rules_text: Rules summary Objective of the Game In Kelp, one player takes the role of the Shark, trying to hunt the Octopus, and the other takes the role of the Octopus, trying to survive. Both players have different goals and paths to victory. The Octopus wins either by surviving until the Shark is exhausted, or by eating all four food blocks. The Shark has only one way to win: by successfully striking the Octopus and beating it in the final confrontation. Anatomy of the Board The board represents a Kelp forest and is divided into different zones. Zones The Exposed Zone is in the center. The Kelp Zones are adjacent to it. The Rocky Zones are in the corners of the board. Shark Den The Rocky Zones include the Shark Dens. On one of these Current spaces the Shark starts the game, and it may also be returned there because of certain in-game actions. Block Space Each zone has a space for the Octopus blocks. Zone Value Each zone has a value that represents the visibility in that part of the Kelp forest. The Exposed Zone has value 2+, the Kelp Zones 4+, and so on - a placed die must be equal to or greater than the zone value. Shark Movement Path The lines represent the path the Shark can follow when it moves. Current Space The blue squares represent Current spaces. The Shark moves on these spaces and can place Current dice on them. Food Track Food blocks are placed here whenever the Octopus eats them. Hunger Track Dice are placed here whenever the Shark uses stored Energy or strikes. Growth Track Formed by the 4 Growth tiles; grants the Shark permanent abilities. Setup This is automated on BGA, but for better understanding see as follows: Fill the Shark dice bag with 7 blue Currents dice, 3 yellow Search dice, and 1 red Strike die (as indicated on the Shark's player aid). Place the remaining dice within reach of the Shark to form the supply. Shuffle the Shark deck, deal 4 cards face-up to the designated row, and place the rest of the deck face-down in the space to its left. Place the 4 Growth tiles with the sides showing the spaces for the dice face-up, in the corresponding numbered slots. From the Octopus cards, remove all starter cards with the special starter symbols and set them aside. Separate the remaining Octopus cards by color and form 4 piles: Learn (blue), Eat (orange), Hide (purple), and Move (yellow). Shuffle each pile individually and place it face-up on the Octopus player's side of the table. Place the matching food block on the top Eat card. Place the other 3 food blocks, 1 shell, 1 double shell, and the 3 traps next to the card piles. Place the hand size token with the number 4 facing up on the space above the draw pile. Place the 3 Shark and 3 Octopus confrontation cards face-down next to the board. Put the remaining 9 blocks (1 Octopus, 1 trap, and 7 shells) into the Octopus bag. The Octopus shuffles the blocks in the bag and draws them one at a time, placing them standing upright in the block spaces (from top to bottom, left to right). Only the Octopus should see the block symbols. Once all blocks are placed, put the bag to the side. Take the card Fast Learning and set it aside. Shuffle the remaining starter cards and place them face-down to form the draw pile. The Octopus takes the starting card Fast Learning and draws 3 additional cards from the starting deck to form the opening hand. The Octopus places the Shark on 1 of the 4 dens, on a Current space, pointing at the center of the board. The game begins. The Octopus takes the first turn. The Octopus As the Octopus, you play cards that let you move stealthily and manipulate the position of the blocks on the board. Most cards come at the cost of revealing blocks, but some cards let you hide them again. Your goal is to survive - win by outlasting the Shark until it is exhausted, or by feasting on all 4 food blocks. Playing the Octopus is a strategic role: manage your available actions and balance the need to move, hide, and even bluff to confuse the Shark. Blocks Adjacency . Blocks are adjacent when orthogonally next to each other, not diagonally. Revealed . Blocks are revealed when they lie horizontally with the icon facing up. Both players can see the icons. Hidden . Blocks are hidden when they stand vertically with the icon facing the Octopus. The Shark should not be able to see the icons on hidden blocks. Actions On your turn, you must take two actions . You may perform the same action twice. There are three possible actions : Play a card . After choosing a card, first pay its cost by revealing the number of hidden blocks indicated on that card. The cost varies between 0 and 3 and must always be paid in full. Each block you reveal usually counts as 1. You can reveal any of your blocks, including food, traps, and the Octopus. After paying the cost, perform the effect on the card. You must be able to complete the full effect to use it; otherwise you can't play the card. Draw back to the size of your hand . You may choose this action if you have fewer cards than your hand size. If your hand is empty, you must perform this action. Whenever you need to draw but your draw pile is empty, shuffle your discard pile to form a new draw pile. You always draw up to your hand size. At the start of the game your hand size is 4 cards. The Octopus does not automatically draw at the end of its turn - drawing is an action . Discard 1 card from your hand, then hide 1 block if possible . Put the discarded card on the discard pile, ignoring its cost and effect, then you may hide one of your revealed blocks. At the end of your turn, move any cards you played to the discard pile. Card Effects There are 4 types of cards: Move . Move cards let you move the blocks around the board in two ways: by swapping or by shuffling . Swapping means exchanging two orthogonally adjacent blocks. They must be swapped in the same state they were in before: a hidden block remains hidden, a revealed block remains revealed. Shuffling means taking a certain number of hidden blocks from the board and placing them into the Octopus bag. Shake the bag and, without looking, pull out the first block (be careful not to reveal it to your opponent). The Shark must indicate an empty spot on the board where you place the pulled block. Repeat until all blocks are back on the board. Shuffling randomizes the blocks - they may end up in the same zone as before, but the Shark doesn't know this. Hide . Hide cards let you stand your blocks back up to hide them again. Hide cards can be played at no cost. Learn . Learn cards improve your skills - improving your deck by gaining better cards and new blocks. For example, Learn 2 lets you gain either 2 new cards, 2 new blocks, or 1 card and 1 block. When you gain a new card, place it on your discard pile unless otherwise stated on the card you played. When you gain a block, you must exchange it with a revealed block on the board. New blocks enter the game revealed. Exchanged blocks are set to the side of the board. You can only gain blocks if you have the required number of revealed blocks on the board . If you gain an Eat card, you also get the matching food block for free. An Eat card and its matching block count as 1 when playing Learn. Some card effects let you trash cards, removing them from the game to make your deck more efficient. Eat . One way for the Octopus to win is to play all 4 Eat cards to eat all the food blocks. To eat a food block, it must first be in play on the board (gained via Learn). Then you must: have the Octopus block orthogonally adjacent to the food block, and have the matching Eat card in your hand. As an action, play the Eat card, then reveal the matching food block and the Octopus (if they aren't already). Now you have eaten. Replace the food block with a spare shell (revealed) and place the food block on the lowest available space on the Food Track. Trash the used Eat card. The Octopus remains revealed until you play another card to hide. Eaten food blocks reward you with a one-time additional free effect (see Blocks below). To activate a food block, turn it face-down to indicate its effect has been used. You can use it before, after, or in between your 2 actions. If you place a food block on the last spot on the Food Track, you win. Blocks Explanation Food effects (activated by the Octopus) Red Rock Crab . Flip the hand size token to 5. Your maximum hand size is now 5 for the rest of the game. In addition, you immediately draw up to your hand size. Sea Snail . You can search your draw and/or discard pile for a specific card and add it to your hand, ignoring the maximum hand size for that turn. After searching the draw pile, you must shuffle it. Cape Rock Lobster . You can immediately hide all your revealed blocks. South African Abalone . You may learn up to 3 for free. Gained cards go to the discard pile; gained blocks must be exchanged with already revealed blocks on the board. Trap effects (triggered by the Shark) Traps are blocks placed by the Octopus but only triggered by the Shark, by revealing them through searching or striking. When triggered, they usually have negative consequences for the Shark. Hide 2 blocks . The Octopus can immediately hide up to 2 blocks. This trap block cannot be hidden with this effect. Discard 1 Current . The Octopus can remove 1 Current from the board. It goes back into the Shark's dice bag. Discard 2 Currents . The Octopus can remove up to 2 Currents from the board. They go back into the Shark's dice bag. Move the Shark to a den . The Octopus moves the Shark to any free den space on the board, positioned like the Shark's starting position. If all dens are covered with Currents, remove one Current (back into the Shark's dice bag) and place the Shark there. Place the Shark at a 90-degree angle to the Shark's path, so the Shark can choose to go left or right. Other blocks Shell . Shells are found scattered throughout the Kelp forest. They have no specific function. Double Shell . The double shell lets you play a card for a cheaper cost. Revealing the double shell is equivalent to revealing any other 2 blocks. Octopus . This block represents you, the Octopus. It can never be removed from the game. The Shark As the Shark, you swim around the Kelp forest from one Current space to the next. You roll different dice to move , search , and strike . With each turn you can become stronger - improving your dice bag and learning new skills - as you chase the Octopus. However, as your skill level increases, so does your hunger for victory: pushing yourself too hard may exhaust you prematurely. The only way to win is by successfully striking the Octopus and beating it in the final confrontation. Playing the Shark is a tactical role: mitigate the luck of the dice and use memory and deduction to keep track of the blocks as they move. Shark Turn Order The Shark's turn has several steps. Only Draw and Roll and Move must be performed every turn, but keep the order in mind: Draw and Roll (2 dice) May place Currents Move Search / Strike Growth Energy Place remaining dice (may get cards) Draw and Roll On your turn, first draw 2 dice from your bag and roll them once. The rolled dice form your pool, which you will place in later steps. Later in the game you may be able to draw more than 2 dice. There are 3 Types of dice: Currents (blue) . Let you place Currents so you can swim faster across the board. Search (yellow) . Let you search for the Octopus by revealing blocks. Strike (red) . Let you strike, meaning attacking a block where the Octopus might be. May place Currents Currents let you swim faster. You may place Currents on any empty Current space, regardless of proximity to the Shark. You may also keep Current dice in your pool to place them later as stored Energy. Move Following the lines, you must move each turn, usually to the next empty space. You can't move backwards, stand still, or turn 180 degrees before moving . You can't stop on a space with a placed Current . By moving over Currents you can swim further, skipping the spaces that have Current dice. You can use a single Current or create chains of Currents to swim even further. A chain of Currents consists of several blue dice placed on connected spaces. However, you can only use a chain of Currents from higher to lower numbers . The numbers don't have to be consecutive , but each die you swim over must be lower than the previous one. After swimming down Currents, regardless of length, remove the first die you swam over and place it on the next empty space on the Growth Track . If there are no empty spaces left on the last Growth tile, put the die back in the dice bag. (By using card effects and stored Energy, you may move more than one space a turn, or even swim the opposite direction.) Search / Strike If you have rolled yellow and/or red dice, you may choose to search and/or strike in 1 or 2 zones to which you are orthogonally adjacent . Placement . The value of each die you place must be equal to or greater than the indicated zone value; otherwise you can't place it and it remains in your pool. Only one die can be placed on a single empty value space. If you have more than one search and/or strike die to place, you must first place both dice and then decide which block will be revealed first. The Octopus must then reveal it. You can also keep the dice in your pool and place them later as stored Energy. Search . Searching reveals the block. To search, use a yellow die. You can only search zones with hidden blocks. Used yellow dice are placed on the next empty space on the Growth tiles; if there are no empty spaces left, return the dice to the dice bag. Strike . Striking reveals the block (if it isn't already) and you attack it. To strike, use a red die. You can strike hidden blocks or, of course, the Octopus if it is already revealed. If you strike the Octopus, immediately proceed to a confrontation. After a possible confrontation or a strike against another block, used red dice are placed on the bottom empty space on the Hunger Track immediately after each strike. Dice placed on the Hunger Track remain there until the end of the game. Additional effects for Search and Strike . If you trigger a trap, its effect comes into play. If you find shells or food, there is no effect. If you find the Octopus with a search die, you now know its position; apart from that, there is no effect. In any case, the blocks remain revealed. Growth The Growth Track grants you permanent abilities. Following the Move and Search step, place the 1st used Current and all used search dice on the next empty space on the Growth tiles, proceeding left to right. Once you have placed 3 dice on a tile, return them to the dice bag and flip the tile. The ability stated on the tile is now always active. After activating all 4 tiles, used Currents and search dice are put back in the bag at the end of the Move and Search steps. Red strike dice can never go on the Growth Track . The Growth abilities (in track order) are : You may reroll one die each turn (before Move). When you use stored Energy but have 5 or less, gain 5 additional Energy (during Energy). You may reroll an additional time each turn (before Move). You may draw 1 extra die each turn (during Draw and Roll). Energy In this step, you must place all remaining dice from your pool in the Energy slots as stored Energy. If you have 1 or 2 dice in stored Energy, you can get new cards. If you have 3 dice stored, you must spend stored Energy to get one or more new cards this round. The sum of the pips (regardless of color) on all your dice in the Energy slots can be used to obtain cards that give one-time special effects and additional dice for future rounds. You can get any number of the available cards whose total cost is equal to or less than the sum of the pips. Each time you get a card, immediately refill the empty spot with a new card from the deck. [Rating: 1/10] Ok gameplay during beginning and middle.  End is so dumb with rock paper scissors deciding the victor.  Needs ending completely reworked. Edit:  So many paid reviews here.  People giving it 10s when they don't even have it.  Designer has an army of people leaving fake reviews and attacking people who leave bad reviews or try to resell their copies.  Shame on them!

[Rating: 1/10] I feel let down by the game, I backed it because I loved the theme and the mechanics seemed really fun to me. Unfortunately I didn't realise the final showdown essentially comes down to a 1 in 3 rock paper scissors style of determining the winner. I absolutely hate such a strategic game essentially coming down to random chance, it makes going through the rest of the game feel like a waste of time. I voiced my opinions on the Kickstarter and I fortunately the creator got really defensive rather than take on my comments, and now I can see lots of other people are having the same issue with the g

[Rating: 1/10] Looked intriguing at first as a hidden-movement game. But then learning the rules, and there's deck-building for the octopus, and dice-bag-building for the shark. There's tedious dice rolling just to determine what the shark can do. And then even when it finds the octopus, you play a rock-paper-scissors game to decide if it's over! Both sides have to build up their engines to get better cards and abilities, and..... so much of this is focused away from hidden-movement!  By the end I was the octopus who had almost nothing hidden. Not because of the stealth game, but because I had to flip tiles 

[Rating: 2/10] I'm just humiliatingly bad at hidden movement games. I felt very constrained in my options... also, I have my usual complaint about a deckbuilding game that doesn't allow me to deckbuild as much as I can in Dominion.

[Rating: 3/10] Der Oktopus muss nur Futter entwickeln und schnell fressen. Nichts anderes. Dann ist das Spiel ganz schnell vorbei. Die Regel sollte da wohl angepasst werden um wieder ein Spiel zu haben. So kann es nicht gemeint sein. Schade. Das Material und die Idee sind schon gut.

[Rating: 3/10] First game ended in 10 minutes due to randomness of tile shuffle, dice rolling, and 1/3 card flip. To me, that is not great design.  Second game shark player rolled two 6s which enabled them on their FIRST turn (thanks to random roll and random market)  bought the 10pt Hostile card. This card trashes 1/3 is the rock paper scissors card, making the win condition for the shart on hit a 50/50 shot.  No thank you

[Rating: 3/10] Bisher empfanden meine Haie das Spiel als wenig intuitiv: Und wenn man sich anschaut, dass das offizielle Regelvideo von Wonderbow rund zehnmal durch Einblendungen korrigiert werden musste (peinlich!), wird da wohl was dran sein.   Wenn man schlecht spielt, kann man leicht in eine Art "Endlosschleife" geraten, welche dazu führt, dass man das Spiel vor dem offiziellen Ende abbrechen muss, da es dem Hai nicht mehr möglich ist, zu gewinnen. Dies fühlt sich für beide Parteien in hohem Maße unbefriedigend an.   Das Deck-Building beim Oktopus macht leider nur wenig Spaß.

[Rating: 3/10] Trotz des enormen Hypes und der hohen Erwartungen, die durch die Kickstarter-Kampagne und die aufwendige Präsentation geschürt wurden, bleibt Kelp spielmechanisch blass. Die Balance zwischen Bluff, Taktik und Glück überzeugt nicht, und das Spielgefühl bleibt flach. Für mich reicht es daher nur für 3/10 Punkte – Kelp wandert wieder in die Bucht.

[Rating: 3/10] There is little more annoying in a board game than spending almost an hour playing a game to have the entire result come down to a coin flip. I could have just flipped a coin an hour ago and saved all that time.
